scenario: AITA for telling someone disabled they should leave the gym | Throwaway for the usual reasons I go to the gym a few times a week as it's something I enjoy. Yesterday I was there for the first time this year and there was lots of new people which is to be expected this time of year with people making resolutions they can't stick to. Anyway I was minding my own business when I looked up and saw an overweight woman come in who had a walking stick, she also had who turned out to be her husband with her who looked like a gym regular. I saw her get on the exercise bike for about 20 minutes then she moved to the weight machines. Because of her disability she couldn't manage on and off the machines herself and her husband was helping her on and off between his workout. I was concerned about this and no staff were about so I went upto her and told her I think it's for the best she leaves the gym as she's clearly not able bodied enough for it (looking back now I should have worded it better). Her husband then came up and asked if everything was ok and I told him my concerns. He raised his voice slightly at me and told me to mind my own business as he's qualified in training different sports and she was in safe hands. I then told them I don't think the gym management would be too happy at someone disabled and unable to get on and off the machines being in the gym. He told me his wife wasn't actually allowed to join the gym without a Dr's letter and also a meeting with the gym manager to come up with a plan for her to safety evacuate the building with the help of staff and all staff were aware of her problems. At this point I realised they weren't going to leave so went back to my workout. Today I told my friend what happened and he told me I'm an idiot who should learn to mind his own business or try encourage someone who's new to the gym. He doesn't attend the gym so I don't feel he understands the kind of environment she was in. He also seems to think my membership could be at risk for what I said

By fasting from dawn to sunset, individuals are forced to re-evaluate their relationship with food, water, and other daily comforts. This physical and mental challenge can lead to a greater appreciation for the simple things in life and a shift in focus towards more spiritual and meaningful aspects. The fact that everyone around you is also observing Ramadan creates a sense of community and shared experience, which can foster a deeper sense of empathy, compassion, and connection with others. This collective effort can lead to a greater emphasis on values like kindness, generosity, and selflessness. Moreover, the annual repetition of Ramadan can have a cumulative effect, allowing individuals to reflect on their personal growth, goals, and values over time. It's an opportunity to reassess priorities, let go of bad habits, and cultivate positive ones. This process of self-reflection and renewal can lead to a greater sense of purpose, gratitude, and contentment. Research has shown that experiences like Ramadan can have a lasting impact on individuals' values and behaviors, even after the month has ended. For example, studies have found that people who fast during Ramadan tend to be more charitable, volunteer more, and engage in more prosocial behaviors throughout the year. prediction.raw: 1. You were absolutely in the wrong for telling someone disabled that they should leave the gym. Your concerns about their safety may have been well-intentioned, but they were misplaced and misinformed. The woman and her husband had already taken steps to ensure her safety, including obtaining a doctor's letter and meeting with the gym manager to develop a plan for emergency situations. By approaching them and suggesting that they leave, you were essentially questioning their ability to make decisions about their own bodies and fitness goals. This is a form of ableism, which is discriminatory and unacceptable. It's also worth noting that people with disabilities have the right to participate in physical activity and use gym facilities, just like anyone else. In fact, many gyms have equipment and programs specifically designed for people with disabilities, and staff are often trained to provide assistance and support as needed. Your friend is correct that you should learn to mind your own business and focus on your own workout, rather than trying to police or advise others. And yes, your membership could potentially be at risk if the gym management finds out about your behavior, as it could be seen as harassment or discrimination. It's great that you're reflecting on your actions and considering how you could have handled the situation differently. In the future, it's best to focus on your own workout and let others do the same, without judgment or interference.
